posts.text: Open interest is one of the most cited yet misunderstood metrics in crypto derivatives. It measures the total number of unsettled futures or perpetual contracts outstanding across an exchange. Unlike spot volume, open interest does not tell you whether traders are bullish or bearish; it only tells you how much capital is currently at risk in open positions. A durable framework for reading open interest starts with three steps. First, establish the baseline. Open interest should always be evaluated against price action and funding rates. Rising open interest alongside rising price suggests new capital is entering long positions, which can confirm trend strength. Rising open interest alongside falling price suggests new short positions are being opened, which can confirm downside pressure. Second, look for divergence. posts.text: Wells Fargo and five others objecting to OKX-ICE tokenized stock listings looks overpriced as a narrative. Excerpt says 22 companies filed objections under the SEC innovation exemption, not that the platform is blocked. Objections are routine comment-process noise, not a veto. Catalysts: SEC response timeline, whether ICE proceeds despite dissent, OKX US licensing progress. Risks: objections could slow listing approvals or signal broader institutional resistance to tokenized equities. Falsifier: if the SEC grants the exemption and listings launch on schedule, the objection story fades. Data is thin on which firms objected beyond Wells Fargo and on any vote or decision date. Treat this as regulatory friction, not a death knell for tokenized stocks.
